  • Sound does indeed reflect off a mirror, but it also reflects off of any hard surface so not specific to mirrors.

  • Gamma do have a higher energy state than visible light photons, which means that gamma rays have a shorter wavelength than visible light. Not longer!

Find a material that won't absorb or interact with gamma radiation. That's your mirror.

You can scatter certain gamma rays off of certain nuclei, but it's all very specific and not very reliable. Also, since gamma rays only interact with nuclei, they pass straight through most materials as if they weren't there.

So the answer is: kind of. If you could have a certain type of nucleus that reliably reflects gamma rays of the wavelength you're interested in, and could make a material dense and thick enough to reflect most gamma rays shot at it, you'd have a (kind of) gamma ray mirror.
